extracted.intended_audience: employers, workplace safety managers, and occupational health professionals responsible for heat-illness prevention
extracted.subtask_description: Implementation and compliance with OSHA's proposed heat-illness prevention standard, including monitoring (heat index or WBGT), development of monitoring plans, employee involvement, provision of water and break areas, and related procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-site monitoring location
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers who choose to conduct on-site monitoring would need to set up monitoring devices at or as close as possible to the work area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May mean setting up the device(s) on a tripod a few yards away from an employee. For multiple work areas at one site, a single device may be used if there is no reasonable anticipation that heat exposure will differ between work areas; otherwise measure at the work area of the employee reasonably expected to have the highest exposure and apply that value to all employees. Employers should follow the device manufacturer's manual when conducting monitoring and ensure devices are calibrated and in working order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of forecasts vs on-site monitors
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers whose employees perform work outdoors must consult the weather forecast or their monitoring device(s)—whichever they are using to comply with monitoring—frequently enough to determine with reasonable accuracy when conditions at the work area reach the initial and high heat triggers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check forecast as close to the start of the work shift as possible; may need to consult again later in the day if conditions change. Use short-term (hourly) forecasts rather than long-term (weekly, monthly). Employers are responsible for ensuring controls required at triggers are in place when those triggers are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement frequency requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitoring devices must be used with 'sufficient frequency to determine with reasonable accuracy employees' exposure to heat.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If forecasts suggest triggers won't be reached, measurements may not be necessary. Where temperatures approach triggers, several measurements may be necessary, especially as the hottest part of day approaches. For WBGT, additional measurements may be needed when air speed or radiant heat change. OSHA requests comment on whether to specify a fixed interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indoor worksite identification for monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: For indoor worksites, employers must identify the work areas where they reasonably expect employees to be exposed to heat at or above the initial heat trigger and then create a monitoring plan to determine when employees in those work areas are exposed to heat at or above the initial and high heat triggers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers could determine areas by consulting previously collected monitoring data, site/process surveys, employee interviews and input, and heat injury/illness surveillance data. Consider areas near heat-generating machinery and whether outdoor temperature increases could raise indoor temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring plan contents and inclusion in HIIPP
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must develop a monitoring plan that covers each identified work area and include the monitoring plan(s) in the employer's HIIPP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan should determine specific times of day, processes, or months when exposures at or above triggers occur, and account for circumstances that impact heat conditions for each work area (e.g., radiant heat sources, air movement). Plan should specify how and when monitoring will occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of monitors 'as close as possible' without inaccuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitors must be set up at or as close as possible to the work area(s) identified, with 'as close as possible' meaning the closest possible location that won't otherwise create inaccurate measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employer should outline appropriate frequency of measurements sufficient to determine exposures. Monitor placement should consider shading, radiant heat sources, and air movement — e.g., WBGT in shade should not be applied to unshaded areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative sampling for multiple indoor work areas
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple work areas are expected to have exposures at or above the initial heat trigger, the employer may conduct representative sampling instead of measuring each area individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using representative sampling, employers must sample the work area(s) expected to be the hottest (e.g., closest to a heat-generating process). Employers cannot place a monitoring device in a work area known or expected to be cooler and consider that representative of other work areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate and update plan after changes that could increase exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: If any changes occur that could increase employee exposure to heat (e.g., change in production, processes, equipment, controls, or a substantial increase in outdoor temperature), the employer must evaluate affected work areas to identify where employees may be exposed at or above the initial heat trigger and update or develop a monitoring plan accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include installation of new heat-generating equipment or a local heat wave increasing indoor temperatures. The employer must update and implement the monitoring plan to account for increases in heat exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee involvement in monitoring determinations and plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must involve non-managerial employees (and their representatives, if applicable) in the determination of which work areas have a reasonable expectation of exposing employees to heat at or above the initial heat trigger and in developing and updating monitoring plan(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employee input can identify processes/equipment that give off heat and times or seasons when areas feel uncomfortably hot; employees often have the most knowledge about their working conditions and their involvement helps ensure accuracy and sufficiency of monitoring plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of heat metric and corresponding triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: The heat metric the employer chooses to monitor (heat index or WBGT) determines the applicable initial and high heat triggers under the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If monitoring heat index, initial trigger is 80°F and high trigger is 90°F. If monitoring WBGT, use the NIOSH Recommended Alert Limit (RAL) as the initial trigger and the NIOSH Recommended Exposure Limit (REL) as the high trigger. Employer must identify which metric they are monitoring in their HIIPP; if they do not, triggers default to heat index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption by assuming exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers who choose to assume that their employees are exposed to heat at or above both the initial and high heat triggers are exempt from monitoring requirements while making that assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These employers would not need to conduct monitoring or keep monitoring records for that period, but they must provide all controls outlined in paragraphs (e) and (f) while making this assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of required protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer is required to provide the specified protections during the time period when employees are exposed to heat at or above the initial heat trigger; additional protections apply when exposures are at or above the high heat trigger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protections apply only for the hours when exposure meets or exceeds triggers (examples given for partial-shift exposures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of potable drinking water
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must provide access to potable water that is placed in locations readily accessible to employees when employees are exposed at or above the initial trigger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Water should be as close as possible to employees to facilitate rapid access; compliance options include water coolers, food-grade jugs on vehicles, bottled water, or refillable bottles. Common-source provision must include a means for employees to drink (disposable cups or refillable bottles). Open common drinking containers (barrels, pails) are prohibited. Employers should keep extra bottles/cups on hand in case employees misplace theirs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water accessibility (location) constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Water is not 'readily accessible' if in a location inaccessible to employees (e.g., inside a locked building/trailer) or placed at a distant or inconvenient location relative to where employees work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break areas and water locations should minimize time needed to access water, which must be paid. Employers should place water as close as feasible so employees in distress can promptly access it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water temperature – 'suitably cool'
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must provide access to potable water that is suitably cool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cool or cold water is more palatable and encourages higher consumption, reducing dehydration and heat strain. OSHA references prior language that water 'must be low enough to encourage employees to drink it and to cool the core body temperature.' Compliance examples: coolers, taps/fountains that maintain cool temperature, ice or ice packs. OSHA requests comment on whether to require a specific temperature range (some states specify temperatures, e.g., 60°F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum quantity of drinking water provided
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must provide access to one quart of drinking water per employee per hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specifies the amount employers must provide, not the amount employees must drink. Employers can comply via continuous-supply taps/fountains or by replenishing coolers/jugs as quantity diminishes. Employers must inform employees about the importance of drinking water during training and when high heat triggers are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost to employee for drinking water and supplies
rubrics_metrics.description: All drinking water requirements must be implemented at no cost to employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers may not charge employees for the drinking water required nor for equipment or supplies needed to access it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electrolyte supplements not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers may choose to offer electrolyte supplemental packets or electrolyte-containing sports drinks, but these would not be required under the standard and would not substitute for providing drinking water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA preliminarily determined electrolyte supplementation may not be necessary in most situations if workers consume adequate meals; stakeholders noted some workers may be unable to consume certain supplements due to sugar content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outdoor break area basic requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When temperatures meet or exceed the initial heat trigger, employers must provide one or more employee break areas at outdoor worksites that can accommodate the number of employees on break, is readily accessible to the work area(s), and has either shade or air-conditioning (if in an enclosed space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break areas must allow employees to hydrate, remove PPE, and cool down. Break areas should permit ventilation/airflow. No minimum square footage proposed, but areas that only fit employees shoulder-to-shoulder or do not allow free movement or access to amenities would not be large enough. Employers must evaluate how many employees are reasonably expected to be on break simultaneously and ensure break area(s) are sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break area accessibility and travel time
rubrics_metrics.description: Break areas must be readily accessible to work areas so employees can take breaks promptly, particularly when experiencing early HRI symptoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break areas requiring more than a few minutes to reach would not be considered readily accessible. Employers should locate break areas close enough to minimize time/effort to access them. For mobile worksites, employers should relocate break areas as needed or ensure each worksite has a break area. Employers must pay employees for time to get to the break area and for break time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shade requirements for break areas
rubrics_metrics.description: If using shade, the break area must have artificial shade (e.g., tent, pavilion) or natural shade (e.g., trees) that provides blockage of direct sunlight and is open to the outside air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shade must block direct sunlight such that objects do not cast a shadow in the shaded area; verifying that employees' shadows are obstructed is sufficient. Shaded break areas must allow air movement across the skin (open to outside air) — e.g., a pop-up canopy with one enclosed side complies; a closed trailer with four sides does not. Employers may use portable or fixed shade and may incorporate fans or misting devices, though not required. Employers may use large vehicles as shade if not running and not part of the work process; equipment used in work processes (e.g., tractors) may not be used for shade due to safety and radiant heat concerns. Employers using shade from buildings must consider path of shade throughout day to ensure coverage and adequate capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air-conditioned break area requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If using air-conditioning for break areas, the break area must be in an enclosed space (e.g., trailer, vehicle, or structure) that is large enough to accommodate the number of employees on rest breaks and be readily available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers using air-conditioned vehicles must ensure the vehicle remains readily available during work periods when the initial trigger is met or exceeded. For mobile employees, breaks in an air-conditioned convenience store or restaurant are acceptable if all other break-area requirements are met. OSHA seeks comment on specifying AC levels and pre-cooling requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and limitations for break area options
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed requirements give employers flexibility to use shade or air-conditioning but also limit certain uses (e.g., cannot use running vehicles or equipment in process as shade).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA acknowledges diverse outdoor industries and workplace layouts, requests comments on allowing indoor break areas for outdoor employees in facilities with both indoor and outdoor work, and on limiting use of indoor break areas to those with AC.
